content: Kidney transplantation is the preferred treatment for patients with end-stage kidney disease. Previous research has demonstrated that the routine use of ureteric stents during kidney transplantation reduces the occurrence of major urological complications (MUC). However, this benefit is accompanied by an increased risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs), which are now the most common complication following kidney transplantation. UTIs pose a significant threat to transplant recipients, particularly those who are immunosuppressed, as is often the case in the context of increasingly complex immunological challenges in transplantation. Different strategies for ureteric stenting are associated with varying levels of morbidity and healthcare costs. This review aimed to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of early versus late removal of ureteric stents in kidney transplant recipients. Early removal was defined as removal before the third postoperative week (within 15 days) or during the initial hospital admission for the transplant. Late removal occurred after this period. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of MUC, while secondary outcomes included the incidence of UTIs, complications related to the stent itself, hospital-related costs, and adverse events. A subgroup analysis was conducted to compare outcomes based on the type of ureteric stent used: bladder indwelling (BI) versus per-urethral (PU). The review included five studies involving a total of 1,127 patients. The overall risk of bias in these studies was judged to be low or unclear, and all studies employed a prospective randomized design. The evidence regarding whether early stent removal reduces the incidence of MUC compared to late removal was uncertain (relative risk [RR] 1.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.61 to 5.71; low-certainty evidence). However, early stent removal may reduce the incidence of UTIs (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.81; moderate-certainty evidence). This reduction in UTI risk was observed only when BI stents were used (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.70; moderate-certainty evidence). In contrast, when PU stents were used, there was no significant difference in UTI incidence between early and late removal groups (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.17 to 2.03; low-certainty evidence). Data on healthcare costs and quality of life outcomes were insufficient. In conclusion, early removal of ureteric stents after kidney transplantation may lower the risk of UTIs, particularly when BI stents are used. However, it remains uncertain whether early removal increases the risk of MUC. BI stents appear to be the optimal choice for achieving a reduction in UTI risk.
